common_name: Alluvial Gold Louisiana Iris (Parent of Bushfire Moon)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Alluvial Gold is a Louisiana iris documented chiefly through its role in breeding: hybridizer Heather Pryor crossed it with 'Gladiator's Gift' to produce the ruffled orange-yellow Bushfire Moon, registered in 1994. Its own flowers follow the broad, flat, fleur-de-lis form typical of Louisiana iris hybrids, growing from vigorous, spreading rhizomes. Plant divisions in full sun along a pond margin, ditch bank, or rain garden low point where the ground stays reliably moist through the growing season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer to keep the planting vigorous and free-flowering.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Gladiator's Gift Louisiana Iris (Parent of Bushfire Moon and Hot And Spicy)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Gladiator's Gift is a Louisiana iris whose lasting significance lies in breeding rather than wide retail availability: Heather Pryor crossed it with 'Alluvial Gold' to produce the orange-yellow Bushfire Moon and separately with 'Desert Jewel' to produce the tomato-red, Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal-winning Hot And Spicy, making it a parent behind two distinct, acclaimed introductions. As with other Louisiana iris, it grows from spreading rhizomes that need consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil and full sun. Site it at a pond edge or rain garden low spot, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer to sustain vigorous rebloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Dural Gold Louisiana Iris (Parent of Percolator)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Dural Gold is a Louisiana iris cultivar best known today as a breeding parent: T. J. Betts crossed it with 'Amanda's Echo' to produce Percolator, registered in 2001, an ochre and nasturtium-orange Louisiana iris that itself went on to influence later Gulf Coast breeding lines. It shares the broad, flat-faced flower form typical of Louisiana iris hybrids, produced on vigorous, spreading rhizomes. Plant it in full sun in consistently wet to moist, fertile soil at a pond margin or bog garden, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain strong bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Amanda's Echo Louisiana Iris (Parent of Percolator)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Amanda's Echo is a Louisiana iris documented mainly through its place in the pedigree of Percolator, the 2001 T. J. Betts introduction it parented alongside 'Dural Gold'. Its own flowers follow the broad-petaled, flat-faced form characteristic of Louisiana iris hybrids, carried on spreading rhizomes that thrive in constantly damp ground. Grow it in full sun with rich, consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil, siting it along a pond edge or rain garden low spot. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer to keep the planting floriferous.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Gold Plaque Louisiana Iris (Parent of Vermilion Queen)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Gold Plaque is a Louisiana iris cultivar remembered chiefly as a breeding parent: Richard Goula crossed it with 'Clara Goula' to produce Vermilion Queen, registered in 1992, a buttery-gold Louisiana iris that itself went on to parent later introductions. Like other Louisiana iris hybrids it grows from spreading rhizomes that need consistently wet to moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil to perform well. Plant divisions in full sun at a pond margin, bog garden, or other low spot that stays damp through the season, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigor.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Myra Arny Louisiana Iris (Parent of Mikal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Myra Arny is a Louisiana iris cultivar whose main documented legacy is as a parent: Mary Dunn used a seedling cross involving Myra Arny to breed Mikal, registered in 1980 and introduced by Bay View Gardens the following year. It shares the broad, flat-faced flower form and vigorous, spreading rhizome habit typical of Louisiana iris hybrids. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet to moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Voodoo Song Louisiana Iris (Parent of Henry Rowlan)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Voodoo Song is a Louisiana iris documented primarily through its role as a parent: M. D. Faith bred Henry Rowlan from a Voodoo Song cross, and Henry Rowlan went on to parent a Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal-winning cultivar in its own right. Like other Louisiana iris hybrids, it grows from vigorous, spreading rhizomes best suited to consistently wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil. Plant it in full sun along a pond margin or bog garden, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to sustain bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Full Tide Bearded Iris (Parent of Glistening Icicle)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; this historic Tall Bearded iris is grown today chiefly for its place in breeding history.

directions: Full Tide is a Tall Bearded iris preserved today mainly for its place in breeding history: William Maryott crossed it with 'President Farnsworth' to produce Glistening Icicle, registered in 1982, a white and true-blue bicolor that itself later parented the border bearded iris Christiana Baker. Detailed records of its own flower color and form are scarcer than its breeding significance, a common fate for mid-century parent cultivars overshadowed by their descendants. Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to full sun in sharply drained soil, since standing moisture quickly causes rot. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: President Farnsworth Bearded Iris (Parent of Glistening Icicle)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; this historic Tall Bearded iris is grown today chiefly for its place in breeding history.

directions: President Farnsworth is a Tall Bearded iris known today chiefly through its role as a parent, alongside 'Full Tide', behind William Maryott's 1982 introduction Glistening Icicle. As with many historic parent cultivars, records of its own flower color and form have faded more than its place in later iris pedigrees. Grow it like other bearded iris, setting rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to full sun in sharply drained soil. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

directions: Dreamcastle is a Tall Bearded iris remembered today mainly as a parent: Paul Cook registered a 1956 seedling of Dreamcastle as Melodrama, which itself stands in the pedigree behind the 1977 American Dykes Medal winner Dream Lover. Documentation of Dreamcastle's own flower color has faded with time, a common fate for mid-century parent cultivars overshadowed by their more famous descendants. Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, since standing moisture leads to rot. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain flowering vigor.

common_name: Golden Isle Tree Peony (Lutea-Hybrid Parent of Golden Era)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, since tree peonies resent being moved once established.

directions: Golden Isle is a lutea-hybrid tree peony documented today mainly through its role in breeding: D.L. Reath crossed it with 'Daphnis' to produce the advanced-generation yellow hybrid Golden Era, which first bloomed in 1971. As a lutea-type hybrid it carries ancestry from Paeonia suffruticosa crossed with the yellow-flowered P. lutea/delavayi group, a lineage prized for pushing tree peony color into warm gold and bronze tones not found in straight Chinese and Japanese suffruticosa cultivars. Plant in a permanent site in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun where summers are mild, or with afternoon shade where summers are hot, since tree peonies resent being disturbed once established. Limit pruning to removing dead or damaged wood, since next spring's flowers form on the current season's mature stems.

common_name: Cassady Grape (Historic Labrusca Parent of Niagara)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Cassady is a 19th-century American Labrusca grape preserved in horticultural history chiefly as one of the two parents of Niagara, which C.L. Hoag and B.W. Clark bred in Lockport, New York in 1872 by crossing Cassady with Concord. Like other Labrusca cultivars of its era, it produces the musky, markedly aromatic flavor distinctive to native American grapes rather than the cleaner profile of European vinifera varieties. Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun and well-drained soil, training to a 4-arm Kniffin or similar system. Prune hard each dormant season, since fruit forms on one-year-old canes, and expect the vigorous, cold-hardy growth typical of Labrusca grapes in short-season northern climates.

common_name: Peloursin Grape (Historic French Parent of Petite Sirah)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Peloursin is an old French wine grape from the Isere region, grown today mainly for its historical role as one of the two parents of Durif, the grape better known in American vineyards as Petite Sirah, which arose as a chance cross of Peloursin and Syrah discovered in the 1800s. On its own it produces a thinner-skinned, earlier-ripening wine than its famous offspring and has become rare even in France, surviving mainly in heritage vineyard collections. Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, training to a permanent cordon. Prune hard each dormant season and watch for bunch rot in humid conditions, since its skin is markedly thinner than Petite Sirah's.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology
